deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of material that later appeared as Ramanujan's 'Highly composite numbers' (Proc. London Math. Soc. 1915). The goal is the order of magnitude of the primes p_r, i.e. how p_r compares with p_1.

Notation (implicit on the page; supplied by me). Write a highly composite number as N = prod_p p^{a_p} with a_2 >= a_3 >= a_5 >= ... . Let p_r be the largest prime whose exponent is >= r. Then N = prod_{r>=1} prod_{p<=p_r} p, so
  log N = theta(p_1) + theta(p_2) + ... , where theta(x) = sum_{p<=x} log p.
Also d(N) = prod_p (a_p+1). A prime with exponent a contributes a+1 = 2 * (3/2) * ... * ((a+1)/a), so
  d(N) = prod_r ((r+1)/r)^{pi(p_r)} = 2^{pi(p_1)} (3/2)^{pi(p_2)} (4/3)^{pi(p_3)} ... .

Step 1 (perturbation). Replace level 1 by primes up to q_1 and level r by primes up to q_r:
  N' = N exp(theta(q_1) + theta(q_r) - theta(p_1) - theta(p_r)).
Then d(N') >= d(N) * 2^{pi(q_1)-pi(p_1)} * (1+1/r)^{pi(q_r)-pi(p_r)}.
This is an equality if the nested structure p_{r+1} <= q_r <= p_{r-1} is preserved. My justification of '>=' in general: if the structure breaks, an affected prime has exponent a >= r+1 rather than r. When the exponent drops, the factor a/(a+1) exceeds r/(r+1). When it rises, the factor (a+1)/a is at least as large as the one assumed. So the inequality holds in every case.

Step 2 (case q_1 > p_1, q_r < p_r). Choose
  pi(q_1) = pi(p_1) + n,
  pi(q_r) = pi(p_r) - [n log2 / log(1+1/r)].
Then d(N')/d(N) >= 2^n (1+1/r)^{-[n log2/log(1+1/r)]} >= 2^n * 2^{-n} = 1.
By definition of highly composite, M < N implies d(M) < d(N). So d(N') >= d(N) forces N' >= N, i.e.
  theta(q_1) - theta(p_1) >= theta(p_r) - theta(q_r).

Step 3 (Chebyshev-type sandwich). For alpha > beta,
  (pi(alpha) - pi(beta)) log beta <= theta(alpha) - theta(beta) <= (pi(alpha) - pi(beta)) log alpha.
This holds because every prime in (beta, alpha] has log between log beta and log alpha. Hence
  n log q_1 >= [n log2/log(1+1/r)] log q_r.

Step 4 (lemma). If pi(alpha) = pi(beta) + x with x = o(beta/log beta), then log alpha = log beta + O(1). This follows from Chebyshev's bounds, since an interval [beta, c*beta] contains >> beta/log beta primes. Applied to both perturbations, it gives log q_1 = log p_1 + O(1) and log q_r = log p_r + O(1). This tacitly requires n = o(p_1/log p_1) and n r = o(p_r/log p_r).

Step 5. Substituting:
  n(log p_1 + O(1)) >= [n log2/log(1+1/r)] (log p_r + O(1)).
Divide by n, using [y]/n = y/n + O(1/n):
  log p_1 + O(1) >= (log2/log(1+1/r) + O(1/n)) (log p_r + O(1)).
Since log2/log(1+1/r) <= (r+1) log 2 = O(r), expanding and dividing by log 2 gives
  log p_1/log2 - log p_r/log(1+1/r) >= O(r + log p_r / n).
Here O(...) means a quantity bounded below by -C(...).

Step 6. Choose n of size about log p_r / r, so that log p_r = O(n r). The page ends here. The next page concludes
  log p_1/log2 - log p_r/log(1+1/r) >= O(r).
The symmetric case (q_1 < p_1, q_r > p_r) gives the reverse inequality, hence
  log p_r / log(1+1/r) = log p_1 / log 2 + O(r).
Equivalently, p_r is roughly p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2}.
errors: The inequality d(N') >= d(N)*2^{...}*(1+1/r)^{...} is stated without justification. It is true (see reconstruction), but it needs the observation that breaking the nested structure only increases d(N')/d(N) relative to the formula.

The lemma 'pi(alpha)=pi(beta)+x, x=o(beta/log beta) implies log alpha = log beta + O(1)' is asserted without proof. Ramanujan first wrote 'easy', which appears struck out. It needs Chebyshev-type lower bounds for primes in [beta, c*beta], and in the negative direction for [beta/c, beta].

The admissibility conditions on n are implicit: n = o(p_1/log p_1) and n r = o(p_r/log p_r). With the eventual choice n ~ log p_r / r these hold only when p_r is large compared with log p_r. Uniformity in r, for r up to the size where p_r stays bounded, is not addressed.
The notation 'X >= O(Y)' is used to mean X >= -C Y. This is an informal but standard Ramanujan/Hardy-era usage, not an error of substance.
The O(1) from replacing log q terms is absorbed into O(r) silently. This is valid since log 2/log(1+1/r) = O(r) and r >= 1.

results.what: Representation of a highly composite N as exp(sum theta(p_r)) and d(N) = prod ((r+1)/r)^{pi(p_r)}
results.modern_name: Structure of highly composite numbers (Ramanujan's p_r notation)
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan, Highly composite numbers, Proc. LMS 1915

results.what: Exchange argument: perturbing the prime levels so that d does not decrease forces N' >= N; combined with theta/pi sandwich bounds
results.modern_name: Local optimality / exchange argument for highly composite numbers

results.what: log p_r / log(1+1/r) = log p_1/log 2 + O(r), i.e. p_r ≈ p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2}
results.modern_name: Asymptotic size of exponents of highly composite numbers: a_p ≈ 1/(p^{log2/log p_1} - 1)

results.what: Sandwich (pi(a)-pi(b)) log b <= theta(a)-theta(b) <= (pi(a)-pi(b)) log a

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of an argument contained in Ramanujan's published 1915 memoir on highly composite numbers, whose manuscript material is well studied (e.g. Nicolas–Robin's annotated edition). It is interesting as a working draft but contains nothing not already attributed to him.

transcription_corrections: Header on the page: 'Add ms a 94 18(52)' and folio number (52) in a circle are omitted from the transcription.
In 'But it is easy to show', the word 'easy' appears struck through in the manuscript, so the transcription '[-easy-]' is appropriate.
In 'n log q_1 >= ...' and 'n{log p_1 + O(1)}', the subscript 1 is overwritten and could be misread (e.g. as q_p); it is 1.
Last line: 'log p_r = O(nr)'; the underline under p_r in the image is a stray mark, not part of the formula.
